newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Eskom probes nuclear power expansion.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Eskom probes nuclear power expansion.

text.p: South Africa's Eskom is investigating the possibility of high-temperature gas-cooled nuclear reactors to help meet future energy demand, a utility executive said on Wednesday.

Nuclear Safety Manager David Nicholls said in an interview that the pebble bed modular reactor (PBMR) project, which Eskom began evaluating in 1993, was one of several "very interesting ideas" for future power generation.
Feasibility studies had reached an advanced stage but no decision had been taken, he said.
Nicholls said the design of the PBMR, developed in Germany over 20 years ago, meant that it was intrinsically incapable of accidents like those at Three Mile Island or Chernobyl.
He said the worst-case scenario for a PBMR was equivalent to the dangers posed by Eskom's conventional coal-fired power stations.

"It looks like the possibility of building a plant based on existing technology which physically can't have a major (safety) event...If you abandon it for more than nine days after the worst accident, you end up with the concrete starting to get overheated, but there's no release of radioactivity," Nicholls said.

The PBMR model being studied by Eskom would cost around 400 million rand and have an output of 100 megawatts, compared with 1,000 mw for each of the two reactors it now operates at Koeberg north of Cape Town. Replacement cost of Koeberg would be around 14 billion rand.
Nicholls said the gas-cooled reactor was much cheaper than the pressurised water type at Koeberg because it did not require the same elaborate safety systems.
A PBMR could be built in two years, giving Eskom more flexibility in meeting fluctuations in electricity demand.
Eskom had massive excess capacity in the late 1980s but is now experiencing high growth in demand.
"We're looking for shorter lead times, more flexible plants," Nicholls said. Because of the ease of fuel supply, a PBMR could be built wherever it was needed, minimising energy loss in transmission.
"You could fit five of them on a football field," Nicholls said.
"Results indicate this option would be highly competitive in the South African situation and its load following capability would balance Eskom's current baseload generation mix."

Five research and demonstration high-temperature gas-cooled reactors have been built in Europe and the United States, but the technology was never fully commercialised. Two are now being built in Japan and China.
Nicholls said that if Eskom went ahead with the PBMR project, it could give South Africa a world lead in the technology and create a major new export industry.
